claims.text: A reactive surface modification will promote in situ formation of a lubricious oxide layer on CoCrFeNi during sliding.
The induced oxide layer will remain stable from room temperature to 800 °C.
The surface modification will maintain low friction and wear throughout the room-temperature-to-800 °C range.
Controlled deposition is a possible route for modifying an HEA surface.
Controlled deposition or surface doping can induce formation of the proposed lubricious oxide on CoCrFeNi.
The lubricious oxide is likely to be enriched in chromium or other alloying elements.
The treatment will produce an ultrathin, continuous oxide layer at the tribological interface.
The oxide layer will act as a protective, low-shear film.
The reactive treatment will enable rapid formation of a self-adaptive oxide tribolayer during sliding.
At lower temperatures, the tribolayer will reduce direct metal-to-metal contact, thereby lowering friction and wear.
At higher temperatures, the tribolayer will prevent deleterious oxidation and excessive wear by providing a thermally robust lubricious interface.
The untreated CoCrFeNi alloy has higher friction and wear at high temperature than at room temperature.
The friction coefficient of as-processed CoCrFeNi deteriorates notably above room temperature.
Treated CoCrFeNi will have lower coefficients of friction than untreated CoCrFeNi at every tested temperature from room temperature to 800 °C.
Treated CoCrFeNi will have lower wear rates than untreated CoCrFeNi at every tested temperature from room temperature to 800 °C.
At elevated temperatures, the treated alloy will approach or exceed the performance of other self-lubricating systems.
The proposed performance is expected only under controlled atmospheres and loads similar to those of earlier studies.
The hypothesis does not make a prediction for substantially different loads or corrosive atmospheres.
